sentences: Every language names certain things and leaves others unsaid; it illuminates some areas of experience while leaving others in the dark, due to a lack of words to express them.
This silence of language, these experiences that our language does not name, raise a troubling question: does what has no name exist for us?
Does the absence of a word condemn an experience to non-existence, or does it persist, silent, waiting for the word that will reveal it?
This question, an extension of our previous reflections, touches on the most intimate relationships between language, perception, and being.
It is certain that language guides our attention, and that what it names, we perceive better.

A language that distinguishes several shades of a color, several states of an emotion, and several forms of a human relationship with specific words makes its speakers more attentive to these distinctions; conversely, what a language does not name tends to go unnoticed, blending into the indistinct.
The word, by naming, carves out experience, makes it stand out, and brings it into existence as an object of attention.
What our language does not name thus risks remaining below our conscious perception, not because it does not exist, but because nothing designates it, detaches it, or makes it noticeable.
But should we conclude that what has no name does not exist at all for us?
That would be going too far.

For we often experience things that we cannot name, confused emotions, vague perceptions, states that have no word in our language and yet are there, obscurely present, demanding a name that they do not yet have.

This experience of the unnamed — this feeling of experiencing something for which words are lacking — proves that experience can precede the word, that it exists before being named, even in the shadows of consciousness.
What has no name is therefore not nothing; it is what awaits its name, what exists in the realm of the obscure, the confused, the formless, before the word comes to reveal and articulate it.
It is here that the creative power of language is revealed.

For naming an experience that has hitherto been unnamed is not just labeling it; it is bringing it fully into existence, pulling it out of the shadows, constituting it as an object of consciousness and thought.
When a new word comes to name an experience that everyone felt but could not express, something happens: this experience, suddenly named, stands out, becomes recognizable, shareable, thinkable.
The word does not create the experience out of nothing; rather, it fulfills it, moving it from the obscure to the clear, from the private to the shared, from the sensed to the conceived.

That is why the creation of missing words is an act of immense significance: it gives full existence to what existed only partially, it makes what everyone felt in the solitude of the unnamed expressible and therefore shareable.
This revealing function of language has an ethical and political dimension that we would be wrong to overlook.

For there are sufferings, injustices, and experiences that, lacking words to name them, remain invisible, unspeakable, condemned to silence; those who endure them feel them without being able to express, denounce, or have them recognized.
To forge the word that names them is to make them exist in the common space, allowing them to be recognized and fought against.
Many struggles have begun with the conquest of a word, through the naming of a reality that the absence of a name kept in the shadows.
The silence of what has no name is not always innocent; it can be the silence imposed on what we prefer not to see, and giving it a name is then an act of justice.
Thus, what has no name occupies a singular status: neither fully existing for us nor entirely nonexistent, it lingers in the twilight of the unnamed, demanding the word that will fulfill it.
Language does not create experience out of nothing, but it reveals it, constitutes it, and brings it from the obscure to the clear.

That is why enriching a language, forging the missing words, and learning the words of another language for what one's own does not express is not just a simple vocabulary game: it is about expanding the realm of the sayable, and therefore of the thinkable, shareable, and existent.

Every word conquered from silence is a region of experience torn from the shadows — and one who learns a new language does not just gain words, but entire sections of a world that their mother tongue perhaps left in the silence of the unnamed.

sentences: A tension runs through modern moral and political thought, which globalization has made more acute: the one between universalism and respect for cultural diversity.
On one hand, the idea that there are universal values, valid for all people everywhere — human rights, human dignity, certain principles of justice — that no culture can legitimately violate.
On the other hand, respect for cultural diversity, for their own values, for their right to be different, against the claim to impose a single model on them.
These two demands, equally respectable, seem to oppose each other; and their conflict is one of the most challenging of our time.
Universalism asserts that there are values valid for all, regardless of cultures, and that in the name of these values, one can judge cultures, condemning their practices when they violate them.

This position has its strength and nobility: it refuses to allow anything in the name of culture, it affirms a dignity of man that no tradition can legitimately violate, it establishes the possibility of condemning oppression, cruelty, and injustice, wherever they occur.
Without universalism, nothing could be condemned in any culture, everything would have to be accepted in the name of diversity, including the unacceptable.
Universalism is what allows us to say that certain practices are unjust, regardless of the culture that permits them.
But universalism also has its dangers, which the respect for diversity highlights.
For the claim to universality can mask the imposition of a particular culture, wrongly presented as universal.

What we consider to be universal values may only be the values of a dominant culture, imposed on others in the name of the universal, in a gesture that has justified domination, colonization, and the erasure of cultures in the name of a universal that was actually particular.
Universalism can be a disguised imperialism, a way of imposing one's culture while passing it off as humanity itself.

Respect for diversity reminds us of this truth: that cultures have their own value, their legitimacy, their right to difference, and that pretending to judge them in the name of the universal can be an arrogance.
How can we move beyond this opposition?
Neither absolute universalism, which would deny any legitimacy to diversity, nor absolute relativism, which would prohibit any judgment, are tenable.
The former leads to the imposition of a single model, to the erasure of differences, to the arrogance that takes its particular for the universal.
The latter leads to the acceptance of everything in the name of culture, to the impossibility of condemning the unacceptable, to a respect for diversity that becomes complicity in oppression.
Between these two dead ends, we must seek a path that recognizes both the existence of some truly universal values and the legitimacy of cultural diversity.

This path may involve a distinction: between a small number of truly universal values, which relate to the fundamental dignity of man and which no culture can legitimately violate, and the immense diversity of ways of living, customs, and secondary values, which pertain to the legitimate differences among cultures.

Thus, there would be a universal core, limited but firm — the prohibition of cruelty, respect for dignity, certain fundamental rights — and, beyond that, a vast realm of legitimate diversity, where cultures can and must differ.

This distinction allows for the condemnation of the unacceptable without imposing a single model, for respecting diversity without accepting everything, and for holding together the universalist demand and respect for differences.
Such a position is not easy to maintain, as the boundary between the universal core and the realm of diversity is difficult to draw and is itself the subject of debate.

But it points to the direction of wisdom: neither the universalist arrogance that imposes its particularity, nor the relativism that renounces all judgment, but the recognition of a restricted and firm universal, combined with respect for legitimate diversity.

This position perhaps aligns with the best of what France has in its universalism when it remains clear-sighted: not the pretension to impose its culture in the name of humanity, but fidelity to a few truly universal values, joined with respect for the diversity of ways of being human.

Believing in the universal without imposing its particularity, respecting diversity without renouncing all judgment: this is the difficult balance that our time demands, where cultures coexist as never before, and where we must learn to defend what is valid for all while respecting what legitimately differs.

sentences: Among the qualities that contribute to a wise and happy life, there is one that is rarely discussed yet profoundly transforms existence: gratitude.

Not the simple politeness of saying thank you, but a deeper disposition, one that involves recognizing what is given to us, perceiving and appreciating the goods of our existence, rather than obsessing over what we lack.
This disposition, which can be cultivated, has a transformative power that we underestimate, and it deserves a place in any reflection on wisdom and the art of living.
Our natural inclination leads us away from gratitude: to desire what we do not have rather than to appreciate what we do have, to focus on what we lack instead of what is given to us.

We quickly become accustomed to our possessions, which cease to bring us joy, while our desires are always directed towards what we are missing; we live in perpetual lack, dissatisfied with what we have, reaching for what we do not have.

This disposition towards dissatisfaction, fueled by habituation and by a society that constantly stirs up new desires, prevents us from enjoying what is given to us, keeping us in a lack that nothing fills.
We have much, yet we continually feel the absence of what we do not have.
Gratitude reverses this disposition.
It involves directing our attention not to what is lacking, but to what is given; to perceive, recognize, and appreciate the goods of our existence that habituation makes us forget.
It helps us see what we no longer notice due to our familiarity: health when we have it, the presence of those we love, the goods we enjoy, the beauty of the world, the simple fact of existing.
Gratitude is this attention to what is given to us, this ability to rejoice in it, to recognize it as a good, instead of taking it for granted and obsessing over what is lacking.
It is a shift in perspective, turning towards the abundance of what is given rather than the emptiness of what is missing.
This shift profoundly transforms the quality of life.

For the one who cultivates gratitude lives in a world different from that of the one who lives in lack: where the dissatisfied sees only what he lacks, the grateful perceives the abundance of what is given to him; where one lives in frustration, the other lives in appreciation.
Gratitude does not change external circumstances; it changes the relationship we have with them, and thereby, profoundly, our experience of life.
It is one of the keys to that contentment which does not depend on what we have, but on how we look at it.
The same fate can be experienced in frustration or in gratitude, and this difference in perspective makes all the difference in happiness.
Gratitude also has a dimension that goes beyond mere well-being, an almost metaphysical depth.

For recognizing what is given to us is to acknowledge that we are not the source of all that we enjoy, that much has been given to us without us having earned or produced it: life itself, the world, those who have shaped us, all this heritage that we did not create.

Gratitude is the acknowledgment of this debt, of what we owe to what precedes and transcends us; it is a form of humility, which recognizes that we do not owe everything to ourselves, that our existence is supported by what has been given to us.
In this sense, gratitude is more than a technique for happiness; it is a truth about our condition as beings who receive more than they produce, who owe to others and to the world what they enjoy.
Cultivating gratitude is therefore an essential part of wisdom.

It’s not about denying what is lacking, the evils, the trials, which are real; nor about settling for a naive optimism that refuses to see the bad; but rather learning to also perceive, and first and foremost, what is given, to rejoice in it, and to acknowledge it.

This disposition, which is cultivated through attention, through the habit of recognizing the goods of one’s existence, transforms the quality of life; it is one of the paths to a contentment that does not depend on circumstances, but on the perspective one has on them.

In a world that heightens the sense of lack, that focuses us on what we do not have, cultivating gratitude, learning to recognize and appreciate what is given to us, is an act of wisdom and almost of resistance — and perhaps one of the keys to a life that, without denying its lacks and trials, still knows how to rejoice in what it has received.

Did he obtain air through chemical means, by releasing oxygen contained in potassium chlorate through heat, and absorbing carbon dioxide with caustic potash?

sentences: We were two friends followed by eight spahis and four camels with their camel drivers.
We no longer spoke, overwhelmed by heat, fatigue, and parched with thirst like this burning desert.
Suddenly one of these men let out a sort of cry; everyone stopped; and we remained motionless, surprised by an inexplicable phenomenon known to travelers in these lost lands.

Somewhere near us, in an indeterminate direction, a drum was beating, the mysterious drum of the dunes; it beat distinctly, sometimes more vibrantly, sometimes weakened, stopping, then resuming its fantastic roll.

The Arabs, terrified, looked at each other; and one said, in his language: 'Death is upon us.' And then suddenly my companion, my friend, almost my brother, fell from his horse, headfirst, struck down by sunstroke.

And for two hours, while I tried in vain to save him, this elusive drum filled my ears with its monotonous, intermittent, and incomprehensible sound; and I felt fear, real fear, hideous fear, creeping into my bones, in front of that beloved corpse, in this hole scorched by the sun between four sand dunes, while the unknown echo cast upon us, two hundred leagues from any French village, the rapid beating of the drum.
That day, I understood what it meant to be afraid; I realized it even better another time...
I don't know anything.
No one knows.

The officers, often surprised by this strange noise, generally attribute it to an echo that is amplified, multiplied, and excessively inflated by the rolling dunes, of a hail of grains of sand carried by the wind and hitting a tuft of dry grass; for it has always been noted that the phenomenon occurs near small plants scorched by the sun, and as hard as parchment.
So this drum would just be a kind of sound mirage.
That's all.

And they lived there, with the shutters closed, doors locked, flowers on the ground, and ice syrups brought to them first thing in the morning.
In the evening, they took a covered boat and went to have dinner on an island.

The smoke from the tar was rising between the trees, and you could see large, thick drops on the river, undulating unevenly under the purple hue of the sun, like floating plates of Florentine bronze.
They descended among the moored boats, whose long, slanting cables brushed lightly against the top of their boat.
The sounds of the city gradually faded away: the rumble of carts, the tumult of voices, the barking of dogs on the decks of the ships.
She untied her hat and they landed on their island.
They settled in the low room of a tavern, which had black nets hanging at its door.
They ate fried smelts, cream, and cherries.

They lay on the grass; they kissed in secret under the poplars; and they wished, like two Robinsons, to live forever in this little place, which seemed to them, in their bliss, the most magnificent spot on earth.

It wasn't the first time they had seen trees, blue sky, grass, or heard water flowing and the breeze blowing through the leaves; but they had probably never admired all of this as if nature hadn't existed before, or as if it had only begun to be beautiful since their desires had been fulfilled.

sentences: Amidst these living plants and under the canopies of hydrophytes, awkward legions of arthropods scurried about, particularly serrated frogs, whose shell resembles a slightly rounded triangle, special birgus found in these waters, and horrible parthenopes, whose appearance was repulsive to the eye.
An equally hideous creature that I encountered several times was this enormous crab observed by Mr.

Darwin, to which nature has given the instinct and strength necessary to feed on coconuts; it climbs the trees along the shore, knocks down the coconut which splits upon falling, and opens it with its powerful claws.
Here, beneath these clear waves, this crab moved with unparalleled agility, while free turtles of the species that frequents the coasts of Malabar slowly navigated between the shaken rocks.
Around seven o'clock, we finally walked across the bed of pintadines, where pearl oysters reproduce by the millions.
These precious mollusks clung to the rocks and were firmly attached by their brown byssus, which does not allow them to move.
In what way are these oysters inferior to the mussels themselves, to which nature has not denied any ability for locomotion?
Captain Nemo gestured towards this prodigious heap of pintadines, and I understood that this mine was truly inexhaustible, for the creative force of nature surpasses the destructive instinct of man.
Ned Land, true to this instinct, hurried to fill a net he carried at his side with the finest mollusks.
But we could not stop.

The ground rose noticeably, and at times my arm, which I raised, exceeded the surface of the sea.
Then the level of the bank dropped capriciously.
Often we turned around high, pointed rocks shaped like pyramids.

In their dark crevices, large crustaceans, perched on their long legs like war machines, stared at us with their fixed eyes, while beneath our feet crawled myriads, glycymeris, aricia, and annelids, stretching their antennae and tentacular cirri to an excessive length.
At that moment, a vast cave opened before our steps, carved into a picturesque pile of rocks covered with all the high-lifes of the underwater flora.
At first, this cave seemed profoundly dark to me.
The sun's rays appeared to fade away in successive degradations.
Its vague transparency was nothing more than drowned light.

sentences: The Betis River flows through a fertile land, under a gentle sky that is always serene.

The land takes its name from the river, which empties into the great Ocean, not far from the Pillars of Hercules, and from that place where the furious sea, breaking its banks, once separated the land of Tharsis from great Africa.
This land seems to have preserved the delights of the golden age.
The winters there are mild, and the harsh north winds never blow there.
The heat of summer is always tempered by refreshing zephyrs that soften the air around midday.
Thus, the whole year is nothing but a happy union of spring and autumn, which seem to hold hands.
The land, in the valleys and in the flat fields, produces a double harvest every year.
The roads are lined with laurels, pomegranates, jasmines, and other evergreens that are always in bloom.
The mountains are covered with flocks that provide fine wool sought after by all known nations.

There are several gold and silver mines in this beautiful land; but the inhabitants, simple and happy in their simplicity, do not even bother to count gold and silver among their riches; they value only what truly serves the needs of man.

The women spin this beautiful wool and make fine fabrics of wonderful whiteness; they bake bread, prepare meals; and this work is easy for them, as one lives in this land on fruits or milk, and rarely on meat.

They use the leather from their sheep to make light shoes for themselves, their husbands, and their children; they make tents, some from tanned hides and others from tree bark; they make and wash all the family's clothes, and keep the homes in an admirable order and cleanliness.

Their clothes are easy to make; for in this mild climate, one wears only a piece of fine, light fabric that is not tailored, and which everyone wraps in long folds around their body for modesty, giving it the shape they desire.

When they are told about the peoples who have the art of making splendid buildings, gold and silver furniture, fabrics adorned with embroidery and precious stones, exquisite perfumes, delicious dishes, and instruments whose harmony enchants, they respond in these terms: These peoples are very unfortunate to have spent so much labor and industry corrupting themselves!
This superfluity softens, intoxicates, and torments those who possess it: it tempts those who are deprived of it to seek to acquire it through injustice and violence.
Can one call good a superfluity that serves only to make men wicked?
Are the men of this land healthier and stronger than we are?
Do they live longer?
Are they more united among themselves?
Do they lead a life that is freer, more peaceful, and happier?

On the contrary, they must be envious of one another, consumed by a cowardly and dark envy, always agitated by ambition, fear, and greed, incapable of pure and simple pleasures, since they are slaves to so many false necessities upon which they depend for all their happiness.

sentences: After a moment, she said, "I have nothing to know, sir." But I had found my words; I exclaimed, "Miss, I have loved you for a year!" She was truly surprised and looked up.
I continued, "Yes, miss, listen to me.
I don't know Morin and I couldn't care less about him.
I don't care if he goes to prison or to court.
I saw you here last year; you were over there, by the gate.
I felt a jolt when I saw you, and your image has never left me.
Believe me or not, I don't care.
I found you adorable; your memory possessed me; I wanted to see you again; I seized on the excuse of that idiot Morin; and here I am.

Circumstances pushed me beyond limits; forgive me, I beg you, forgive me." She was searching for the truth in my eyes, ready to smile again; and she murmured, "Joker." I raised my hand, and in a sincere tone (I even believe I was sincere): "I swear to you, I'm not lying." We were alone, completely alone, Rivet and my uncle having disappeared into the winding paths; and I made a real declaration to her, long and sweet, pressing and kissing her fingers.
She listened to this as something pleasant and new, not quite knowing what to believe.
I ended up feeling troubled; thinking about what I was saying; I was pale, oppressed, trembling; and gently, I took her waist.
I spoke softly to her in the little curly hair by her ear.
She seemed almost lifeless, so lost in thought she was.

Then her hand met mine and squeezed it; I slowly pressed her waist in a trembling and ever-growing embrace; she didn't move at all; I brushed my lips against her cheek; and suddenly, my lips, without searching, found hers.
It was a long, long kiss; and it would have lasted even longer if I hadn't heard a "hum, hum" a few steps behind me.

sentences: O Aceste, if the misfortune of young Télémaque, who has never fought against the Trojans, cannot touch you, at least let your own interest touch you.

The knowledge I have gained about omens and the will of the gods tells me that before three days have passed, you will be attacked by barbarian peoples, who come like a torrent from the heights of the mountains, to flood your city and ravage your entire land.
Hurry to prevent them; put your people under arms, and don't waste a moment bringing the rich herds you have in the countryside inside your walls.
If my prediction is false, you will be free to sacrifice us in three days; if, on the other hand, it is true, remember that one should not take the life of those from whom one receives it.
Aceste was astonished by these words, which Mentor spoke to him with a confidence he had never found in any man.
I see well, he replied, O stranger, that the gods, who have dealt so poorly with you in all the gifts of fortune, have granted you a wisdom that is more valuable than all prosperity.
At the same time, he delayed the sacrifice and quickly gave the necessary orders to prevent the attack that Mentor had threatened him with.
All around, there were only trembling women, bent old men, small children with tears in their eyes, retreating into the city.
The lowing cattle and bleating sheep came in droves, leaving the lush pastures, unable to find enough barns to take shelter.

It was a cacophony of people pushing against each other, who could not hear one another, mistaking a stranger for a friend in the chaos, and running without knowing where their steps were leading them.
But the leaders of the city, believing themselves wiser than the others, imagined that Mentor was an impostor who had made a false prediction to save his life.
Mentor displayed in his eyes a boldness that astonishes the proudest warriors.
He took a shield, a helmet, a sword, a spear; he organized Aceste's soldiers; he marched at their head and advanced in good order towards the enemies.
Aceste, although full of courage, could only follow him from a distance in his old age.
I follow him more closely, but I cannot match his valor.
His armor resembled, in battle, the immortal aegis.
Death ran from rank to rank everywhere under his blows.

Like a lion from Numidia, devoured by cruel hunger, who enters a flock of weak sheep, he tears apart, he slaughters, he swims in blood; and the shepherds, far from helping the flock, flee, trembling, to escape his fury.

sentences: Well, said Andrea, you see, the situation would be for the best, assuming that my request is not rejected by Madame Baroness Danglars and by Mademoiselle Eugénie.
We are now in charge of a rental income of one hundred seventy-five thousand livres.

Let's suppose one thing, that I obtain from the marquis that instead of paying me the income he gives me the capital (it wouldn't be easy, I know that well, but still it is possible), you would make those two or three million work for us, and two or three million in skilled hands can always yield ten percent.
I never take less than four, said the banker, and even at three and a half.
But for my son-in-law, I would take five, and we would share the profits.

Well, splendid, father-in-law, said Cavalcanti, allowing himself to be carried away by the somewhat vulgar nature that, from time to time, despite his efforts, broke through the veneer of aristocracy he was trying to cover them with.
Oh!
excuse me, sir, he said, you see, just the hope alone drives me almost mad, what would reality be then?

But, said Danglars, who, on his side, did not realize how this conversation, initially disinterested, was quickly turning into a business deal, there is surely a portion of your fortune that your father cannot refuse you?
Faith, said Andrea, I assure you, sir, that I have never focused my mind on this subject, but I estimate it at two million at least.
Well, sir, said Andrea, bowing to the banker with tender respect, may I hope...
Mr. Andrea, said Danglars, hope, and rest assured that if there are no obstacles on your part to halt the progress of this matter, it is settled.

Said Danglars, you see that while I don't share, in general terms, your sympathy for frankness, I submit to it when I believe the circumstances invite me to do so.
I will continue then.
I proposed a husband to you, not for you, because in truth I wasn't thinking of you at all at that moment.
You love frankness, there you go, I hope; but because I needed you to take this husband as soon as possible, for certain business arrangements that I am currently establishing.

"It's as I have the honor to tell you, my daughter, and you mustn't hold it against me, for it's you who force me into this; it's against my will, you understand, that I enter into these arithmetic explanations, with an artist like you, who fears to enter a banker’s office to perceive unpleasant and anti-poetic impressions or sensations.

"But in this banker’s office, which you were kind enough to enter the day before yesterday to ask me for the thousand francs that I grant you each month for your whims, know, my dear young lady, that one learns a lot about the very use of young people who do not wish to marry.

For example, one learns, and out of respect for your nervous sensitivity I will tell you this in this salon, that a banker's credit is his physical and moral life, that credit supports a man just as breath animates the body, and Mr.
de Monte-Cristo once gave me a speech on this that I have never forgotten.

One learns that as credit withdraws, the body becomes a corpse and that this will happen very soon to the banker who takes pride in being the father of such a good logician." But Eugénie, instead of bending, straightened up under the blow.

--You have found the right expression, my daughter, the right expression, said Danglars, scratching his chest with his nails, while maintaining on his rough face the smile of a heartless man, but not without spirit, ruined!
That's it.
Yes, ruined!
Well then, it is now known, this secret full of horror, as the tragic poet said.
